Against the keen, lone, throbbing sky;
The tang of the old box
Fills the clear dusk from wall to wall,
And the dews fall.
Come back!

I watch, I cry:

Leave the rude wharf, the marts,
Come back!
Else shall break my heart
And I am forgot:

Oh days as they were not!—
The warm, sweet, grooming tunes,
The Sunday afternoons,
Wrought but for you;
The larkspurs growing tan,
You wreathed in pink and blue,
Within your prayer-books small;
The cupboards carved both in and out
With curious, prickly vines
And smelling far and near;
The pictures in a row,
Of folk you did not know;
The toys, the games, the shrill, gay rout;
The lanterns, that at hour for bed,
A charmed but homely red,
Went flickering from shed to snow;
The fagots crumbling, spicy, good,
Brought in from the great wood;
The dark that held you all about;
The wind that would not go?—
Come back, my women and my men,
And take them all again!

the people to take hold of this proposition and push it through. A plant could
be put in here and maintained at
small cost, perhaps cheaper than in
most places, and we believe it would be a
paying investment. The people are
the ones who should own and control
affairs of this kind, and if we sit around

and let some one come in here from the
outside and put in a plant, we cannot
blame anyone but ourselves. It is true
there are not many people here who
have enough money so they can take
stock in a company of this kind, but
there are enough who do have the necessary cash, but are not willing to invest it in such a proposition. Consequently there is always some opposition
here to a movement that is started and
advocated by the people. How to overcome this we are not able to say.


Quite a number of our prominent citizens are bitterly opposed to the idea of
letting outside capital be brought here
for the purpose of installing an electric
light plant, but in a great many cases
their reasons are not justified. Let us
suppose that a company from Salt Lake
came here with money to put in a $1,000
or $5,000 plant, and they took the power
into Salt Lake, would the people here
have to pay more for their lights than
if they owned the plant themselves?
We think not, nor perhaps as much. If
the people themselves put in a plant
they will have to take enough lights to
keep the thing going, and perhaps thus
the lights would cost them a great deal less
than they are now paying for oil. On
the other hand, if the plant was owned
by a Salt Lake concern and it was not
depending entirely on the support
they would get here, the company could afford to let us have light at a reasonable
figure. If we thought the price was too
high, there would be no compulsion
about taking the light.


A city the size of Coalville could support an electric light plant if the people
were all united in establishing the same,
but so long as this division is manifested on the part of some of our prominent citizens nothing will ever be accomplished that will result in good for us.

I got my first bruise before I had been in the service sixty days. That was at Perryville, Oct. 5, 1862. We were lying down behind a rail fence when a bullet from the rifle of a rebel sharpshooter struck a rail right above my head, flattened out like a pancake, glanced off in my direction, struck me on the shoulder, leaving a black and blue spot as big as my hand. That bullet hurt me worse than if it had gone through me, and yet was reported bruised, not wounded."

"Again at Shiloh, at Chickamauga, a flattened ball or a piece of shell grazed me so close as to bruise and blister the skin, and again I got no sympathy and was laughed at for not tallying a hit. At Buell's Roost in May, 1862, we fought in an open field from early morning before daylight until 5 o'clock at night. Along in the afternoon, tuckered out with the heat and the hot weather, I squared myself behind a tree for a rest.

I told the boys I was going to take a nap. This was meant to be a joke, but, sitting against the tree, I went to sleep, my head wobbled to one side, exposing my camp-kettle hat, and a johnnie put a bullet through the hat so close to my head as to cut the hair. I awoke with a start, to be laughed at by the boys. I got another scratch at Kenesaw and a blister or bruise at Peach Tree Creek, and other at Jonesboro, but I got no further. Tough on any of them I can't truth. Many say that I was wounded, and yet that bruise on my shoulder troubles me to this day."

"I had worse luck than that," said the sergeant. "On the night our division crossed the Tennessee river in the march on Chattanooga, in September, 1863, I met with the queerest mishap that ever befell a soldier. I had been on heavy duty for two days and nights and it seemed to me I couldn't keep awake another minute. All of Bragg's army came sweeping down the surge through which we were moving. I remember looking up at the ruins of the high bridge and trestlework at Falling Water, between Shellman's and Lookout mountain. Then all was blank.

I had some to sleep, walking. We were marching in fours, rides as a nightwatchman shift, and the men on either side stood shoulder to shoulder. So for a time I slept and walked, when a turn came in the road the mechanism in my body, set for going ahead, stopped, and I went down like a log, my knee striking me a cruel blow and my face striking the rough ground. I carry the marks of that day, but the men of that old company would call me a fraud if I should say I was wounded at Falling Water."

"My most painful wound," said the Captain, "did not come from bursting shell, or rifle bullet or saber cut. Going up Missionary Ridge, I was close behind a great big fellow, who pushed his way through brush and abattis. Out of the manner of my frightened ball, at one point he bent forward the sharpened points of a branch of a fallen tree, and, releasing himself, let the sharp points hit my back. right in his estimate of the distance

season, however, will do up the best
of them. Then they drift to the four
wheelers.

Senator Hanna has rested fairly well since morning. Temperature, 102 4/10, pulse, 92.

Senator Hanna rested well. Temperature, 101; pulse, 82.

The temperature is regarded as the more important indication in the course of the fever, which runs in cycles of seven days. Probably the oldest method of determining the time of day was by the sundial, but other devices have been used for ages, including the water clock, the burning wick and the hourglass filled with sand. Popular legend attributes to King Alfred the invention of the water clock, but long before his time it was in use by the Egyptians, and in Judea, Babylon, Chaldea and Phoenicia. The contrivance for measuring time by means of water appears to have consisted of a basin filled with water and exposed in some niche or corner of public place. At the extreme end of the vessel was a spout or tap, from which trickle the liquid drop into a reservoir, having on its inside marks indicating the hours of the day and night.

In parts of southern Asia there was used a thin copper bowl about twelve inches in diameter and rather deeper than half an inch, having a few small holes in its bottom. Water poured in a vessel containing water as it escaped through the small holes at regular intervals, and every an hour watcher struck a cone at each time to show the lapse of periods of hours with great accuracy, but the time varied with the temperature of its water. You were participators in the tragedy and now almost half century afterwards when the graves of your comrades are grown over and green with the verdure of spring, when the scars of war are becoming obliterated, when a new generation has come upon the stage of action, you the remnant of that mighty host, the grizzled veterans of battle and conflict and storm come together here to pay loving and tender tribute to those who have gone before you. It is a solemn, beautiful and sacred service. It may do no special good to the dead, but I am one of those who believe that from their tents and camping grounds on the other side of the river they are not unmindful of their survivors and their friends, and it is no stretch of imagination to feel and believe that their spirits may be with us here today. If this is true it will comfort them to know how well and kindly they are remembered, to know the results of their work and the immeasurable blessings which have come upon the country and its people on account of their labors and sacrifices. Henry Weeks, son of Hon. E. w.
Weeks, has received through Senator
Allison, the appointment of cadet at
West Point military school. He is
ordered to report at Fort Sheridan,
Chicago, on May Sd for examination,
and if successful will go to West
Point on June 4th. His friends have
no doubt but what he will safely pass
the mental and physical examination,
as his ambition for the past few years
has been to enter West Point, and he
has been bending his energies towards
preparing for that event if it happen
ed. He also has desire to make as
good grades and record as his uncle,
Lieutenant d. H. Bower, who gradu-
ated in the class of 1902, and who is
now stationed in the Philippines.
The Guthrian.

Call it illusion, hallucination, phantom or
what you will, such sight was lately be-

psychology and psychurgy, near Chevy
Chase according to Prof. Elmer Gates, the
director.


I obtained the strange story from Prof.
Gates's own lips yesterday. He told it thus:


"I have been experimenting with some
light rays about five octaves above the vi-
olet—a form of wave energy somewhat akin
to X-rays but about as different from
them as they are different from sound.
This new radiant force is invisible when
produced in an ordinary room, but I sue-
ceeded in making it visible by projecting it
upon a wall coated with a substance whose
color is altered by the action of the rays
in question.


This substance was rhodopsin—the visual
purple of the retina, the seeing substance of
the eye which light acts upon. This rho-
dopsin I extracted from the eyes of freshly
slaughtered animals. I find that all known
inorganic and inanimate substances are
transparent to this force. Unlike the X
rays, they will shine through metals, bones
and such substances which I can hold be-
tween the tube emitting these rays and the
wall covered with rhodopsin without ther-
e casting a shadow, so to speak, or causing
the color of the wall to be changed over the
corresponding area.


I find that any living thing, however, is
opaque to these rays, and that it will cast
a shadow as long as it retains life.
A live rat is placed in a theoretically
sealed glass tube held in the path of these
rays and before the sensitized wall. As
long as the rat remains alive it casts
a shadow. On killing the animal it is found
after certain lapse of time that it becomes
suddenly transparent.


THE SHADOW ASCENDING.
At the same instant a shadow having
precisely the same shape as the animal is
seen to pass out through the glass tube and
move upward on the sensitized wall.
Two of my laboratory assistants claim
to have distinctly seen the shadow in the
full course of its ascension. As soon as we
can definitely prove this to other scientific
men we will have demonstrated that some
organism, presumably not atomic, perhaps
etheric and capable of passing through
glass, thus leaves the atomic body of an
animal. If such an organism could be caught and made to give evi-
dence that it still possessed mind, then we
would for the first time have an induc-
tion, a laboratory proof of the continuity of life.
How do you now account for the opaque
ness of the living organism under these
rays, to which all lifeless matter is trans-
parent?" I asked the professor.


"I can best answer that after describing
another experiment," said he. "I arranged a
room lined throughout with thin sheets of metal
connected with the earth by electric con-
ductors passing through a galvanometer
sufficiently sensitive to measure the amount
of electricity emitted by any person in the
room.


The body has its every muscle and nerve
electrically excited whenever exercised.
Every muscle and nerve is an electric con-
ductor. If I lift my arm, thus, and keep
the muscles tense, they give off more elec-
tricity.
During exercise of the mind there are
similar electric discharges into the sur-
rounding atmosphere. By quantitatlvely
measuring the electric waves given off by
a person in mental activity we can effect
some measurement of that activity by
measuring the electric waves given off by
it.


If you have a more intense emotion of any
kind than have I, of that same emotion
you will give off more electric waves while
exercising that emotion than will I. Thus
if I were to take two brothers separately
into the lead-lined room, announce to each
the news that his mother had died, the
galvanometer would show in whom had
excited the strongest emotion of grief.
This is the first time in the history of
psychology that there has been any con-
ceivable method of comparing subjective
states.


But to return to the rat in the tube, my
explanation of its opaqueness while alive
is this: In any living body there are elec-
tric waves hurrying in all directions
through the nerves and muscles. Light
waves which are electric waves, cannot
penetrate such a bundle of electric waves.


Do you think, then, that the life fluid is
an electric fluid, as many aver?


I think that life is some unknown force;
electricity is one. Life or mind is more in-
timately connected with matter through
electric force than through any other.


CAN THE GHOST BE CAUGHT?


"Do you hope to catch that organism
which left the dying rat and cast its shad-
ow on the wall?"


I am unwilling to discuss in detail my
experiments in these as yet unknown fields
until after they shall have been further in-

successfully made then biology and psychol-
ogy will have been extended across the
border without an intervening chasm, and
the continuity of personal identity beyond
death will have been scientifically demon-
strated."

immortality of the soul?"


"No, it would not demonstrate endless ex-
istence—merely the continuity of life be-
yond what we call death.


The visible animal organism is com-
posed of atomic solids, liquids and gases.
May there not be etheric solids, liquids and
gases, whose particles are enthusiastically
smaller than atoms, and might there not be
an etheric body composed of them, might
be asked. Such truth could be made a co-
ordinate part of the growing body of scien-
tific knowledge.


In the judgment of nearly every scien-
tist in the world such demonstration of the
actuality of another life has not yet been
made.

held to-day by the United Confederate
Veterans Union. The memorial ad-
dress was delivered by Bishop Gailor
Of the Episcopal diocese of Tennessee.
For the first time since the organiza-
ton was formed General John B. Cor
don. the beloved commander in chief,
whose body rests in Oakland Gene
terry at Atlanta, did not preside. That
his presence was sadly missed was
apparent from the frequent reference
to his many years of service as the
head of the organization and his bril-
liant war record.


LEE WELCOMES VETERANS.

surpassed the achievements Of our fathers

/ deplore the irreparable loss 10 my country
and the coming generation when those splen-
did men, the bravest and best the world
has ever held. went down in death. But It
IS a great comfort TO know that the South

regarded as the god of all natural forces.


II. Elijah fed by ravens (vs. 2-6).
Lame. How. We know not. God's OBJ-
ECT was to protect Elijah from the rage
of Ahab and Jezebel. 3. Leave Samaria
and "Withdrew from the haunts of men"
"Hide thyself." For the king that sent to
every land to find him (1 Kings 18: 10)
would take every possible means to com-
pel him to speak the word of power that
would bring rain. When God intended to
send rain He bade Elijah to show himself
to Ahab (chapter 18: 1). "Brook Cherith."
A torrent bed, deep ravine, down which
in rainy times a strong stream flowed. The
situation of Cherith has not been identi-
fied. It is probable that Cherith was east
of the Jordan. Eusebius and Jerome
place it there. 4. Commanded the ra-
vens. This plain, positive statement de-
fies all attempts to explain the facts stat-
ed in verse six on rational or natural prin-
ciples.


5. Did according. He took the word
of the Lord in the hand of faith as the
staff of his pilgrimage, and journeyed for-
ward and, whenever he grew weary, he
leaned upon his staff, and his strength
revived; and when danger threatened him
by the way, in view of this staff he was
not afraid. 6. Ravens brought him. The
bringing to Elijah of suitable food was
evidently miraculous. "Bread and flesh."
Ravens feed on insects and carrion them-
selves, yet they brought the prophet
man's meat and wholesome food. As this
was the food appointed by the Lord for
the prophet, we may conjecture that it
was the food of the people. 7. "After
a while" Probably about a year "Brook
dried up." If this stream had not dried
up, he would not have been brought thither for water, and thus his
retreat would have been discovered.


III. Elijah at Zarephath (vs. 8-16).
"Zarephath." The Sarepta of Luke 4: 26
was a city of Sidon in the dominions
of Ethbaal, Jezebel's father. It was very
much as if one flying from a lion was di-
rected to seek refuge in a lion's den. "A
widow woman." The condition of the
widows in the East is helpless in the ex-
treme, so that to receive support from
such a source would be another trial to
Elijah's faith. It was like leaning his
weight on a support as frail as a spider's
web.


8. As he did. His COURSE was not TO
reason and to speculate, but to hear and
obey. "Gate." The abject poverty of the
widow is seen from her coming forth to
pick up chance bits of wood which might
have fallen from the trees outside the
city walls. "The widow." A widow. R.
V. It was the widow whom God had
commanded, but Elijah at first saw only
"a" widow, not then knowing this was the
one God had designated. "A little wa-
ter." His first need after his long jour-
ney through famine stricken Israel would
be water. The gift of water to the thirsty
is always regarded as a sacred duty in the
East. Then, too, as Guthrie says, this
test would let Elijah know whether he had
found the one to whom he had been sent.


9. "As she was going." She readily
went at the first word. She objected not
at the present scarcity nor asked what he
would give for a draught, nor limited he
was a stranger, but left gathering sticks
for herself to fetch water for him. Nor
sign of bread. No doubt the prophet was
sadly in need of it; doubtless, too, he was
listening for divine directions. 10. "Thy
God liveth." She recognized Elijah as a
worshiper of Jehovah, and her words in-
stead of fear were faith. 11. "Smallest
kind of bread." A fat, oval cake
of unleavened dough about ten inches in
diameter. "Meal." Wheat, ground in
hand mill. "Barrel." An earthen jar.
"Oil." Olive oil, to eat with bread as
we do butter. "Cruse." A flask for li-
quids. "Two sticks." As among the Ger-
mans at this day two was then equiva-
lent to a few. "Eat it, and die." The
famine prevailed there, and she was in the
last extremity.


13. "Fear not." Have no fears about
the future; trust God. First, this was
a test of her faith in God, and would show
whether she was worthy of the help Eli-
jah offered. It was necessary in order to
make the provision for her wants a real
blessing. Here is faith manifested by
this poor heathen woman such as was not
found in Israel. Jesus found similar
faith in a woman of this same land (Matt.
15: 25). 14. "Barrel not waste,
ETC." A special miracle, but God's com-
mon way of providing for man's common
wants is wonder daily repeated. The
teeming earth is like one vast granary
which God keeps ever full. "Until the
day." It is supposed that he was in Zare-
phath about two and half years. 15.
"Went and did." The increase of this
widow's faith was as great a miracle in
the kingdom of grace as the increase of
her oil in the kingdom of providence.
16. "WASTED not." Here was an exhibi-
tion of that same divine power that in the
person of Jesus multiplied the loaves and
fishes.

themselves alone, they unlocked the
door, and slipping through it, locked it
again on the further side and cropped
their way to the moonlit mouth of the
cave. Here they stood awhile study
ing the descent of the gulf as best they
could in that light, till suddenly God
win, feeling a hand upon his shoulder,
started round to find himself face to
face with Masouda.

"By road which is your only hope,"
she answered. "Now, Sir Goodwin,
waste no words, for my time is short,
but if you think that you can trust
me—and this is for you to judge—give
me the Signet which hangs about your
neck. If not, go back to the castle
and do your best to save the lady
Rosamund and yourselves."

Thrusting down his hand between
his mail shirt and his breast, Goodwin
drew out the ancient ring, carved with
the mysterious signs and veined with
the emblem of the dagger, and handed
it to Masouda.

"You trust indeed," she said with
a little laugh, as, after scanning it
closely by the light of the moon and
touching her forehead with it, she
hid it in her bosom.

"Yes, lady," he answered, "I trust
you, though why you should risk so
much for us I do not know.
Well, perhaps for mates'
sake, for Sinan does not rule by love;
perhaps, because, being of wild blood,
I am willing to set my life at hazard,
who care not if I win or die; perhaps
because you saved me from the lioness.
What is it to you, Sir Goodwin, why
a certain woman-spy of the Assassins,
whom in your own land you would spit
on, chooses to do this or that?"

She ceased and stood before them
with heaving breast and flashing eyes,
a mysterious white figure in the moon
light, most beautiful to see.

Goodwin felt his heart stir and the
blood flow to his brow, but before he
could speak Wulf broke in, saying:
"You abuse us, spare words, lady
Masouda, so tell us what we must
do."

"This," she answered, becoming calm
again. "Tomorrow night about this
hour you fight Lozelle upon the narrow
way. That is certain, for all the
city talks of it, and, whatever chances,
Al-je-bal will not deprive them of
the spectacle of this fray to the death.
Well, you may fall, though that man
at heart is a coward, which you are
not, for here courage alone will avail
nothing, but rather skill and horse
manship and trick of war. If so, then
Sir Goodwin fights him, and of this
business none can tell the end. Should
both of you go down, then I will do
my best to save your lady and take
her to Salah-ed din, with whom she
will be safe, or if I cannot save her,
I will find her a means to save her
self by death."

"You swear that?" said Wulf.
"I have said it, it is enough," she
answered impatiently.

"Then I face the bridge and the
knave Lozelle with light heart," said
Wulf again, and Masouda went on.

"Now if you conquer, Sir Wulf, or
if your fall and your brother con-
quers, both of you—or one of you, as
it may happen—must gallop back at
full speed toward the stable gate that
lies more than a mile from the castle
bridge. Mounted as you are, no horse
can keep pace with you, nor must
you stop at the gate, but ride on, ride
like the wind till you reach this place.
The gardens will be empty of feasters
and of cup-bearers, who with every
soul within the city will have gather
ed on the walls and on the housetops
to see the fray. There is but one fear:
by then a guard may be set before
this mound, seeing that Salah-ed-din
has declared war upon Al-je-bal, and
though yonder road is known to few,
it is a road, and sentries may watch."

Phoenix, Ariz. Oct. 7.—According to
the most reliable advices obtainable re-
garding the troubles at Morenci min-
ing town in Graham county, over the
alleged attempt to sell foundlings from
New York, the situation is not as ser-
ious as has been reported. Available
advices from Clifton, a town near Mo-
renci, are that 40 children were sent
out by the New York Foundling and
Orphans asylum. Sixteen of these were
placed in families in Clifton, and are
taken to Morenci where the majority
of them were placed with poor Mexi-
can families. The American residents
of Morenci objected to the children be-
ing placed with a class of Mexicans
whom they claimed were entirely un-
fitted to have care of them. An indigna-
tion meeting was held in Clifton
and resulted in the arrest of G. W.
Swayne, the agent of the asylum, and
the local priest. The people demanded
that the children be put in the care of
American families, but Swayne refused
to do this and says he would take them
to New York. Objection was made to
the giving over of the children into
Swayne's charge, as it was feared by
some that they might be taken to old
Mexico.


The latest authentic report is that
Swayne is awaiting instructions from
the asylum officials in New York.


The purpose of Swayne and as-
sistants seems to be to place the
children with Catholic families in
this section, of whom there are
but few except Mexicans. While
charges have been made that
the children were being sold, there
appears to be nothing to substantiate

For ages May day has been time Of
general rejoicing. All over Christen-
dom its advent is hailed with delight.
The birds, the bees and the flowers
join us in an annual celebration of the
day. Nature has at last thrown off the
snow quilt with which she has braved
the ravages of winter and glows re-
splendent in buds and blossoms. The
streams have broken their icy letters
and burst forth into joyous accompani-
ments to myriads of bird choristers,
And humanity, overpowered by the
same glad spirit, seeks the woods and
the fields to revel in the wealth OF YER
dure so lavishly spread out


Among the Romans this feeling found
vent in their Floralia, or forea games,
which began on the 28th of April and
lasted several days. We read that
nations taking more or less their orr
gin from Rome have settled upon the
1st of May as the special time for
fetes of the same kind. With ancients
and moderns alike it was an instructive
rush into the fields to revel in the bloom
which was newly presented on the
meadows and the trees"


The barbarous Celtic populations held
a heather festival on this day, but we
are not told that it was in any way
connected with flowers. It was called
Beltein and was celebrated by kindling
fires on the hilltops at night. Within
the remembrance Of many the peasant
ry of Ireland, the Isle of Man and of
the Scottish highlands also held SINH
lar celebrations.-Tab Talk.

HE car was almost due at the suTl-

 init of the Gornergrat. The chill air from the glacier fields pressed stimulating finger on the pulses. The ice of the surrounding glaciers was dull green and deep.

 The Little Traveller, wound to the neck in thick plaid shawl, stood wait ing with her aunt. They were going down on the last car which made the trip that day. They had wished to spend the night on the top, for Elizabeth, the captain of this brief summer outing, had but to give. the orders and Die Tante obeyed like a soldier.

 But, alas, the money was lacking. They had added once and again the col- umna in their account book, and the result came ever the same, with the ttreaome infexibiIity of mathematics. The two hungry sightseers were at last enjoying Switzerland after months of longing. But their rule must be kept -so many marks day, and prices at the tip-top houses have all the rarity of the altitude where they flourish. So this pleasure must be given up.

 For once I am almost satisfied, sighed Elizabeth. Tt, would be too glorious to see sunrise here, too. We must be content with our half-loaf."

 The electric car came slowly creeping up the steel way, bringing noise, dis turbing element, taste of modern im- provement, into these silent heights.

 Elizabeth's green touring hat bore pun of feathers on quivering. wire. Each time they trembled, If you cared for Elizabeth you must look to see if she, too, trembled. "One look, dear aunt, one long look to fix this picture in my mind. How dull the four walls and the sewing will be after this feast ot ice and snow. Just see how clear the air is, and how near the other peaks look. 1 am going to that rock to look at the Matterhorn. There is time to spare. The car is not up yet, and it waits before going down again. Come"

 The rose color of the afterglow on snowy summits defies1< the common sense. Even the solid fields of white, sloping down the channels between soaring peaks, these have a chilled sorcery of their own. Imprint the scene on your mind, Elizabeth. It will always 0IeSJs 4G ASS as yOu SeyS 6O uduuLlUS1y beautiful and remote.

 The dependence, the influences of daily life is the chain by which the spir- itual delights must be confined. And no joy is sufficient to itself, even observa- tion of the Gornergrat panorama The little Swiss watch, delicate toy, the price of which had shortened the pleas. ure trip two weeks, the watch pinned on Elizabeth's breast, continued tick ing and ticking, leading time captive, and leading Elizabeth and her aunt from the rock with its mighty outlook back co the little station. The car stood ready for the descent, with perhaps a 30 sec- onds to spare.

 The morning of the same day George Werner, young student, had arrived at zermatt. His face was long by na- ture, and now it was long from fatigue --and what else? Perhaps it was fatigue alone. He was always jolly in con- versation, therefore he must be always happy. A smile came quickly to his face when he met friend, When lett alone 1t died quickly away But always his interest in others was there

 Young blood must flow a little faster at seeing the noble view which is the hearts desire, George had dreamed of this hour, and now as he sat on the ascending car, here was reality. His reddish hair blew back from his tenn pies, white from the confinement or study.

Omaha, Neb., Dec. 25.—The Union Pacific and Burlington railroad, insisted by the United States government, have a new scheme for reclaiming the several hundred million acres of arid western lands, without the aid and assistance of expensive irrigation work. Dir. Ewooe Mean, head of the agricultural departments in Washington, will represent the government in the deal, and is in Omaha now, conferring with the general managers of both railroads to details of the work, which will begin in the spring.

The new scheme is based on grasses and new alfalfa which grows in south Russia and which requires so little moisture as to exist wherever sage brush and prairie grass can live. Experimental stations will be built at once along the railroads, and from these the surrounding country will be seeded with the new alfalfa. If the scheme is successful hundreds of millions of acres will be added to the tillable lands west of the Missouri River.—Denver News.

From the above it has been seen that Uncle Sam and the railroad companies have a plan for reclaiming land in the semi-arid localities of the west. If they have what is claimed for them in the line of forage plant, there is no question but the introduction of it in this western country would prove of great benefit in retaining the lands of the plains. It is called an alfalfa and we naturally conclude that it must be somewhat similar to the alfalfa raised under irrigation, only very probably not of so large growth. Buffalo grass as forage plant cannot be surpassed considering the smaller size; it makes but the great drawback in depending upon it to furnish forage for stock country to the fact that its small growth forces the stockman to own a tract of land that is not, on of all reasonable proportions to the number of stock grazing upon his range. The new alfalfa will enable the stockman to do business on a smaller acreage and at the same time furnish him with winter feed; it will revolutionize the stock raising business of the plains and soon thickly settle this great territory with small stock men.

Again, if this new forage plant is what it is represented to be, we are justified in concluding that, during the growing season, it would furnish feed for hogs. The great drawback to the hog raising industry in this country has been found to be the great difficulty in securing green feed for the hogs during the growing season. When it comes to keeping hogs in dry pens and feeding corn or other grain the year through, the result is neither good for the growth and health of the hog nor for increasing the revenue of the hog raiser. With good summer forage for hogs, the hog raising industry in this plains country would be a more profitable business than even the cattle business. Judging by the results, this climate cannot be surpassed for this industry. Cholera, the dreaded disease of this industry, is practically unknown to this locality and, so far as we can tell, to all of eastern Colorado. In the last few years, the only case of hog cholera reported in this county was at Holyoke and the hogs had been shipped in from some point in Nebraska to fatten and really had the disease before they were brought into this state.

The experiments with this new forage plant will be watched with much interest by the people in our county, for its success may mean much to them and anything that can be done to aid in this movement will be done.

ceived here sustains Judge Rogers,
who, while sitting for Judge Hook, in
August, 1903, decided that the fran
chise had been improperly terminated
and enjoined the city from interfer
ing with the company in its work of
extending and making repairs on its
lines.


Normal University Burned.—The
normal university at Salina was des-
troyed by fire on September 4. The
building and its contents, with the ex-
ception of piano, an organ, and some
smaller articles, are a total loss. The
university building was erected in
1884 by stock company of local bus
iness men. Recently the majority of
the stock became the property of Prof.
Charles Swisher and G. H. Barnes,
president and principal, respectively,
of the school. The building cost,
originally, $4,000. President Swish
er estimated the value of the contents
at $4,000. The insurance on the
building and contents amounts to
about $4,000.


Rolling in Fat—It is remarkable to
notice the splendid condition of the
cattle of Kingman county. It is im-
possible to find a cow brute that is
not rolling in fat, and the grasses are
just getting at their best stage for
fattening purposes. Cattle will go in
to winter in better shape this fall than
ever before in the history of Kansas,
and there is such an amount of feed
of all kinds raised this season that
it will be an easy and cheap matter
to carry the stock through the winter
in fine shape.


Aid Normal Pupils.—At a meeting
of the stockholders of the Salina
Normal University, which was des-
troyed by fire, no definite action was
taken concerning rebuilding, but the
chances are that the school will not
be rebuilt this fall. President Roach,
of the Kansas Wesleyan, said he
would take care of all the students
that had come to attend the Normal
and the Wesleyan agreed to fulfill
the contract made by the Normal
with each student.


Couldn't Nominate.—Though a pub
lic call was published at Salina for sev
eral weeks for a county prohibition
convention to be held, but one man,
F. C. Sexton, appeared at the hall
where the convention was to have
been held. Mr. Sexton is the candi-
date for Congress on the prohibition
ticket from that district. He went
home feeling rather sad at the pros
pects.


Sow More Wheat.—The farmers of
Coffey county are planning to sow an
unusually large acreage of wheat this
fall. Practically all of the river bot
toms will be put in wheat. They
think the indications point to a good
price for wheat next year and in that
case wheat will bring more money
and quicker than any other crop.
Kansas farmers want all that is due
them about as soon as they can get
it.


Injured by Ball.—At Wichita Harry
Herman, ball player, was hit on the
head by thrown ball. He was in-
jured so badly that for time he was
unconscious and his condition is re-
garded as critical.


Hurt in Runaway—At Topeka, W.
H. Ables, farmer, 60 years old, was
knocked out of his wagon in a runa-
way, sustaining injuries which will
likely prove fatal. His spine was bad
ly injured.


Pioneer Minister Died.—Rev A.
Wahlin, for seventeen years the pas
tor of the New Cortland Swedish Luth.
eran church in McPherson county, is
dead.


Killed by Train.—W. S. Stallings, a
well to do farmer, aged 62 years, liv-
ing six miles west of Fredonia, was
found dead on the Frisco track with
both arms and one leg mashed off
when endeavoring to reach home, he
was caught by an extra freight. He
leaves a family, daughter of 15 and
widowed mother. He was buried with
I. O. O. F. honors.


Finally Agreed.—McPherson coun
ty several high schools have agreed
on course of study after years of
difficulties. Man is slow to coop-
erate as civilization is to advance.


Burning Stacked Wheat.—The burn
ing of several stacks of wheat belong
ing to a Sedgwick county farmer near
Derby may result in trouble for some
one. A telephone message was sent
to Wichita asking that bloodhounds
be sent to Derby to try to run down
the persons who it is thought are
guilty of setting fire to the stacks.


Light Docket—The September term
of the district court of Greenwood
county convened at Eureka September
6. The jury is to be called the Fri-
day. Aside from few small crimina
l cases the docket will be very light.


For U. S. Museum.—Dr. F. H. Snow
of the University of Kansas, has re-
turned from a summer trip to the
canyons of Arizona. He brought bac-
k with him 10,000 specimens of insect!
for the museum of the university. Dr.
Snow has made eight summer trips
for the purpose of adding to the mus
eum collections, and has brought in
a total of 4,000 specimens. Many of
them have been found in new science.


Republican Club—A Young Men's
Republican Club has been organized
at Winfield with 100 members.

If the Convention decide that the judicial quality is the one which prudence and patriotism suggest for the most effective opposition to jinglism and swashbuckling, the man is an almost ideal candidate.
The man from St. Louis.

If the duties should be simply reform in administration, the exposing of wrong and the pursuit and conviction of wrongdoers, the man who has won national fame as prosecutor in St. Louis seems to possess every quality necessary to insure success. His record is absolutely unique, so far as known, in the history of the country. He is a reformer of singular efficacy, and at the same time a politician of consummate skill, while as reformer and politician he has been successful in an extraordinary and almost bewildering degree. Reformers have been numerous, but no other, to my knowledge, has ever been equally successful in fighting rogues in the criminal courts and in the political primaries.

Reformers who are really anxious to end wrongdoing have always been numerous. Reformers who have undertaken to prosecute crime in the courts have not been few. Reformers who have succeeded in obtaining convictions are rare, though not wholly unknown. But the only man, so far as known, who has pursued criminals in the courts to conviction and at the same time has fought them successfully at the primaries, who has actually succeeded in dislodging them from the political scal control in which he found them and in the dissensions that control himself, is the prosecuting attorney of St. Louis.

That he has vindicated Justice in the courts would have been highly creditable, but that he has actually enthroned it in control of a political party so completely that delegates charged with the task of rewarding its champion by nominating him to the highest Office in the Commonwealth will dominate the State Convention of Missouri almost unanimously is an event unprecedented in the history of politics so far as known, and fraught with the promise of measureless benefit to the people of the whole country.

Moral Fibre of the People.

The moral fibre of the American people has always been sound. The virtuous have always been in the vast majority, but their very superiority has tended to make their employment the most extensive and therefore the most exacting, while the less worthy whose time was less valuable, devoting it wholly to politics, have managed to influence largely, if not to dominate, the management of both political parties.

The man who can enthrone the virtuous elements of his party in the control of its management will not be without imitators in the other party. If the country at large should show its approval of his course by bestowing on him the supreme honor of the Presidency.

If both political organizations were managed and controlled by the best element of each, the effect on government would be enormous. Its Foundation would have acquired a new security, its flag new glory, its prosperity an extent which at this moment no man can conceive.

It would be an inspiring spectacle to see the Republican candidate who makes a practice of denouncing political boodlers between elections, but employs and utilizes and courts them at the primaries, opposed by a man who fights political boodlers at primaries and sends them to State prison between elections.

If the delegates to St. Louis think that abilities of the highest order, firmness absolutely unswerving, courage absolutely undaunted, patriotism absolutely unswerving, experience wide, ripe, successful are the qualities necessary to make candidacy successful, the embodiment of them all will be tended to its attention by the delegation from Massachusetts.

Hard to Forgo Cleveland.

Of course there is one man whose election I would be absolutely certain, but the opposition to his nomination is so strong as to make it impossible. The men now prominent in the management of the party have nearly all risen to prominence denouncing him, and of course that makes it almost impossible for them now to accept him as candidate. If the opposition was based on anything he had said of them it might be overcome, but it would be almost superhuman if these gentlemen forgave Mr. Cleveland the harsh things they have said of him. It is very easy to forgive my neighbor anything he may have said of me, but almost impossible to forgive him the things I have said about him. Of course, it must be admitted that the existence of this opposition to Mr. Cleveland in his own party to some extent impeaches his capacity for leadership.

Mr. Cleveland served two terms as President. After the first he left the White House with his party unanimously and enthusiastically attached to him. After the second he left the White House with his party inflamed against him with almost equal unanimity. He served in Congress during half of each administration, and enjoyed more or less intimacy with all its members, especially during the first half of the second term.

Cleveland as an Obstacle.

From my observations, I should say that Mr. Cleveland's greatest quality is not as a leader, but as an obstacle. Bottom, Sept. l6.-The center of
what might rightly be called an
equinoctial storm passed so closely to
the New England coast yesterday that
the shift of wind which followed its
rapid progress to the northeast was ao-
countable for many marine disasters.


The wind attained the velocity of a
hurricane at many exposed points,
such as Block Island, Nantucket and
Highland Light. All of these points
reported velocities of more than sixty
miles an hour from the southeast, fol-
lowed by shift, inside of a few min
utes, to the northwest, from which
direction the wind blew with even
greater intensity.


1t is believed that the disturbance
will be accountable for property
loss east of New York amounting to
more than $1,000 900, and several
lives.

Bonnet shouted back at Ben: "What are you talking about, you driveling idiot; haven't you told Mr. Marchand that I am a pirate?"

"Indeed hae no—" cried Ben, "for I don't believe ye are ane; at least, no to your friends and neebours."

To this Bonnet made a violent reply, but it was not heard. The two vessels had now touched and the crowd of yelling pirates had leaped upon the deck of the Amanda. Bonnet was not far behind his men, and, sword in hand, he rushed towards the spot where stood the merchant captain with his crew hustling together behind him. As there was no resistance, there was so far no fighting, and the pirates were tumbling over each other in their haste to get below and find out what sort of cargo was carried by this easy prize. Capt. Marchand held out his hand. "Good-day to you, friend Bonnet," he said. "I had hoped that you would be one of the first friends I should meet when I reached port at Bridgetown, but little thought to meet you before I got there."

"Friend Marchand," he said, "I see that you do not understand the state of affairs and Ben Greenway there I should have told you the moment we met you. I am no longer a planter of Barbadoes; I am a pirate of the sea, and the Jolly Roger floats above my ship. I belong to no nation; my hand is against all the world. You and your ship have been captured by me and my men, and your cargo is my prize. Now, what have you got on board, where do you hail from, and whither are you bound?"

Capt. Marchand looked at him fixedly. "I sailed from London with cargo of domestic goods for Kingston; thence, having disposed of most of my cargo, I am on my way to Bridgetown, where I hope to sell the remainder."

"Your goods will never reach Bridgetown," cried Bonnet; "they belong now to my men and me."

"What!" cried Ben Greenway, "ye speak without sense or reason. Hae ye forgotten that this is Mr. Abner Marchand, your fellow-vestryman and your senior warden? And to him do ye talk, takin' ava his goods and legal chattels?"

Bonnet looked at Greenway with indignation and contempt.

"Now listen to me—" he yelled. "To the devil with the vestry and da' the Scotchman's eyes and mouth were surrounded with horror that Bonnet stopped and changed his form of expression—" "confound the senior warden. I am the pirate Bonnet, and regard not the Church of England."

"Nor your friends?" interpolated Ben.

"Nor friends nor any man," shouted Bonnet.

tee appointed last August by former
Governor Taft to investigate the laws
and conditions with regard to opium in
all Oriental countries, has rendered it's
report. The committee recommended
that the opium traffic should be strictly
a governmental monopoly at once, that
at the end of three years the importa-
ton of opium should be absolutely pro-
hibited with the exception of medici-
nal requirements, only confirmed hab-
tues Of the drug who are over twenty
one years of age to be granted smok-
er's license, and that an educational
campaign against the use of opium
to be started in the schools.

be termed the essentially Celtic qualities—alertness,

seeks modern methods of increasing its circulation
and of increasing the interest of those who are al-
ready its subscription books. One of the most
effective of these is the proverb contest, the results

that should represent the fine achievement and the
noble side of Irish inspiration.

contest is that the mind is exercised in one and
what is popularly labelled the nerve is exemplified
in the other.

Our callousness to the higher forms of mental
activity is depressing. It means loss of the right
sort of influence. It spells disaster to the aspira-
tions that the best among us have cherished. It
illustrates the contention made through some papers,
repeated in conversations, limited in business
circles that the Irish qualities are not as efficient
as their essential importance would seem to imply.
If they are allowed to continue the Irish race in
certain respects will be to be the subject of an
empty boast when its eulogists claim that it seeks
the best—that its energy is based upon its intelli-
gence.

undue importance to what is, in the last analysis,
scarcely worth serious consideration. It might be
said that the mind of the Irish-American of Bos-
ton is stirring along other lines than the mere
unravelling of puzzles.

indication of mental lassitude too seriously. It is a
dictated drift in the current of our mental life that
has not escaped the attention of discriminating ob-
servers. In fact, if the matter were clearly put, it
might be said that the Irish-American took little
interest in a proverb contest because he was fa-
miliar with the proverbial wisdom that the good
sense and the hard-won experience of generations
have put into form.

It expresses their humor, their philosophy of life,
their spiritual outlook. It is valuable because it is
taken from the heart of life. It is not the result
of closet-study but represents the last word that
crisis has forced some perchance unlettered man to
say.

books. This is the chief reason, in the view of the
Republic, that more Irish-American names are not
found in the list of honor.

for the life among books. The great names of lit-
erature are dim to our eyes. We do not realize
that while the spiritual life must be fed by the sa-
craments and prayer, there must be food for the
imagination, the judgment. A book-
less house is desert. Yet we ignore books. If it
were not for the exalted thought and the great spirit-
ual purposes which the confessional conserves, we
should be aground in the race. Fortunately the
church with the sacraments, its appealing ritual,
the vividness and efficacy of its ethical teaching,
supplies for the place that books hold in the heart
and mind of those not in the union of faith.

book dwellers, but there is a great need that the young
should have their minds stored with reasons for the
faith. A well-chosen book is solace and an in-
spiration. It is a perpetual and good friend.

was rather, we fancy, a difficult person to get on
with. He was rather grim and decidedly intoler-
ant. But there was a touch of iron in his blood
and the realization in the background of his brain
that a bookless race is an inferior race. He set up
his house and his barn and dug his ditches and
prayed God's vengeance upon those who differed
from him. But he also set up his printing press.
And the printing press is the mighty mother of
civilization.

His descendants created a multiform and high
civilization that was based on books. They made
history that is full of great deeds and noble names.
They developed literature that embraces the clas-
ses of this country. Three centuries have passed.

books? You have but to look around you to see.

nations would scarcely use for pasture boasts
the greatest colleges, the best-equipped technical
schools, the most amply endowed libraries, the most
fruitful civic institutions in the western he-
misphere.

The Irish American strain has energy. It tin-
kles with energy. But undirected energy is not
enough. We must have carefully-formed intel-
ligence directing it, frowning upon its mistakes and
leading it to better objects of development.

The white beggars, organ grinders and loiterers of San Francisco have learned this, and they observe the day more religiously than they observe the Christian holidays. On the morning of the great Chinese festival they go down to Chinatown and invade the narrow streets in battalions, wearing their most doleful expressions.

The Chinese, passing up and down the sidewalks, throw them coins, sometimes by handfuls. In California, it must be remembered, there are no pennies.

Sometimes a big merchant, a "first chop" man, comes along and gives to each mendicant he meets no less than half a dollar. Then there is a scramble of the lame and the blind, some of them collecting half a dozen times. Exchange.

Superior to All Other Breeds.

The herd of Jersey cows assembled at the World's Fair at St. Louis to represent the Jersey breed in the universal dairy test has been inspected and has been pronounced in perfect condition and ready to start upon their six months grind on a day's notice.

W. R. Spann of the Burr Oak Jersey farm, Dallas, Tex., was the inspector, and he was thorough in his work. He passed a week on the Exposition grounds, and much of the time was spent in and around the Jersey cattle barn, and the condition of each individual of the herd of forty cows was definitely ascertained.

Never was more intelligent and careful treatment lavished on animals. No athlete was ever better trained for a contest requiring the development of speed, skill and endurance than has been this herd of Jerseys. When it is known that this herd is to compete with selected herds of Holsteins, Shorthorns, Brown Swiss and Devons, and the herd making the best score for production of butter, milk and cheese is to establish the standing of the various breeds, the importance of the cows being in perfect condition may be understood.

For a solid year the Jerseys have been in constant training. Twenty-five cows will participate in the contest. Cows were selected from the best herds in the United States.

Prof. J. J. Richardson, president of the American Jersey Cattle Club, under whose auspices this entry is made, toured Europe and visited the famed Isle of Jersey, where the breed originated. He was seeking the best cows, but returned satisfied that Europe could show no cows that were better than those bred in America.

Though only twenty-five cows will participate in the test, forty cows were selected. They were assembled at Jerseyville, Ill., a year ago. This is near St. Louis, and the cattle have become acclimated. Last December they were removed to St. Louis. The cows are the property of individual members of the club and are loaned for the term of the test. C. L. Graves, a breeder at Maitland, Mo., was selected as the superintendent to have charge of the cattle, and he has been highly complimented by Prof. Richardson and inspector Spann for the wonderfully fine condition in which he has placed the herd.

A series of model dairy barns have been built for the breeds competing in the test. The barns are octagonal in form, and are so arranged that the cows are in the center and wide promenade permits visitors to pass around and view the cows as they stand in their stalls.

The milking and feeding are to be done in plain view of the public and representatives of the various herds will at all times have access to all the barns to see that no sharp practices are induced.

The test not only consists in showing the amount of butter, milk and cheese produced, but the cost of production is taken into consideration. Every ounce of food given each cow is weighed and carefully recorded. When the cows are milked, the milk is conveyed to a model creamery in the Agricultural building, where it is tested and made into butter and cheese and where all records are carefully kept.

The Jersey cattle participated in a similar test at Chicago during the Columbian Exposition and carried first honors.

Superintendent Graves is sanguine over the result of the present test. He says that the Jerseys have always demonstrated their superiority over all other breeds when placed in competition, and this time they will show to better advantage than ever. Not only is the Jersey milk richer in butter fat than the milk of any other breed, says Mr. Graves, but it can be produced at a less cost. The Jersey cows are the smallest of the standard breeds, and he asserts that they consume less feed. They assimilate their food, and it is converted into milk and butter and is not used in building up and sustaining a large carcass.

"We are going to make all other breeds take to the woods after this test," said Mr. Graves. "A few days ago I was testing some of our Jersey milk, and my hands were all sticky and greasy from the enormous amount of butter fat the milk contained. Mr. Woueyne, who is in charge of the Holsteins, sent over a quantity of his milk for me to test. Of course, from a commercial standpoint there was no comparison between the milk, but it was a pleasure to test his milk, for when I got through there was no grease on my hands. After this I have a bucket of Holstein milk around handy to wash my hands in after testing our own rich Jersey milk."

The test begins May 1st and continues for six months.

| hand 1T was occupied by friends of
Fred nj. Warner. 1t was ten year ago
that his constituents sent him to the
senate. They were satisfied with his
record and returned him for another
term. The Detroit News said of him
at the end of both term that he was a
man who had not been controlled by
the machine" In 1898 he came up
for the nomination for secretary of
state and was defeated by Justus s.
Stearns. He turned in and did his best
for the success of the ticket. Two years
later he came MP again for the same
Office and was nominated. For the last
four years therefore he has occupied
that Office and never for an instant
during that time has there been spot or
blemish on his name or on any of his
official acts. At next Christmas time
Fred M. Warner will go to Lansing to
take the oath of Office as governor of the
State of Michigan and for the next four
years there will never come any blush
of shame to the face of any Michigan
citizen for any act of their chief execu-
tive.


So don't trust the democratic party
too far with its plea for primary re-
form. Like the many other measures
which it has fathered for a, time, only
to disown later when discredited by
the people, the present issue is simply
one on which it fondly hopes to sail in
to power, one which it hopes to make
the means of destroying the united ef-
fectiveness of the republican organiza-
tion and one on the details of which the
members of its own party are widely
disagreed except as to the advantage of
making it present means of attacking
the republican candidate for governor
in this state. You have seen the party
quickly abandon one after another dis
credited issue which it had successively
claimed to be paramount to all other
issues Don't trust it too far with this
one.


Congressman Joseph W. Fordney was
then introduced to the audience and the
speech which he made was full of his
usual mixture of plain common sense
and contagious good humor. He was
certain. he said at the outset, that if
there were any persons present who
had been in favor of primary reform as
advocated by the democrats they must
have been in the condition of a certain
Irishman after they had listened to the
hsmocratic candidate attempt to ex-
pound his theories. 1t was the Irish
man who dressed in hurry and jump
ed out of third story window to escape
burning in hotel. He did not notice
in his haste that he had got into his
trousers with the front where the back
should be and announced to his inquir-
ing friend after the jump, and after he
had looked and felt himself over, that
he was mot hurt but dom bodily twish-
thed. ," He thought however the ad-
dress just given by Mr.. Fellows was
one well calculated to take the ''twisht"
out of the minds of the audience in re-
gard to the primary reform plans of the
democrats.


Mr. Fordney took occasion to call to
mind one Of the strange contradictions
on which Mr.. Parker is making his
claim for election. In one instance the
Judge said that even if he were elected
and even If democratic house were
also elected they would be powerless to
do anythi 4 for the next four years be-
cause the Senate would still remain re-
publican. In the next place he tells the
country that if elected he will positive
ly decline to be a candidate for reelec-
ton. Therefore his claim for the cleo
tion SINNERS down to plea that if
elected he will be unable to do any in
jury because he will not be able to do
anything the first term and will not
take. a second term. Nice sort of a
policy that indicates.


Mr.. Fordney then discussed briefly
and in most interesting way some of
the subjects of national interest in
which he had taken the greatest inter
est, touching on the healthy condition
of the United States treasury which
shows an enormous gold reserve and a
big balance of cash on hand even after
just having paid fifty millions for the
Panama canal He spoke briefly of the
great benefit the republican party had
conferred on the country districts by
the rural free delivery service which
the democrats had tried to discourage
and suppress. The Panama canal and
the vigorous course of the president in
making certain that the policy Of Presi-
dent Mckinley and the wishes Of the
American people in regard to 1t were
also gone over and the reasons given for
complete approval of the course of the
president in the matter.


Our president, said Mr.. Fordney. does
not take forever TO make mp his mind.
And yet contrary to the impression that
his enemies would like to make, he is a
conservative executive, with an able
council about him, one of whom, in my
opinion, is the ablest statesman in the
world today, Secretary of State, John
Hay. The nations treatment OF the
Philippines was reviewed briefly as
was also that of Porto Rico and Cuba,
while the subject Of pensions to the old
